content: Dental caries, commonly known as tooth decay, is a prevalent condition that can be prevented by reducing the consumption of free sugars and using topical sodium fluoride products. Chlorhexidine, an antibacterial agent, has been proposed as a potential preventive measure for dental caries. Various chlorhexidine-based products, available in different formulations and concentrations, are either sold over-the-counter or administered professionally. While some previous reviews have suggested that certain chlorhexidine formulations may slow the progression of existing caries in children, there is insufficient evidence to confirm or deny its effectiveness in preventing dental caries. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of chlorhexidine-containing oral products, such as toothpastes, mouthrinses, varnishes, gels, gums, and sprays, on the prevention of dental caries in children and adolescents. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, up to February 25, 2015. No language restrictions were applied. After removing duplicate citations, 1,075 references were identified. The review included only parallel-group, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared the caries-preventive effects of chlorhexidine products with placebo, no treatment, or other chlorhexidine formulations in children and adolescents. Studies combining chlorhexidine with fluoride or comparing chlorhexidine to fluoride interventions were excluded. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Disagreements were resolved through consensus, and trial authors were contacted for clarification or additional information when necessary. Due to the clinical diversity of the included studies—such as differences in participant age, intervention composition, outcome measures, and follow-up periods—meta-analysis was limited. In cases where meta-analysis was not feasible, a narrative synthesis of the results was provided. The review included eight RCTs that investigated the effects of chlorhexidine varnishes (1%, 10%, or 40% concentrations) and chlorhexidine gel (0.12% concentration) on the primary and/or permanent teeth of children aged 0 to 15 years at the start of the studies. A total of 2,876 participants were randomized, with 2,276 (79%) evaluated. Six studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias, while two were deemed to have an unclear risk of bias. Follow-up periods ranged from 6 to 36 months. Six trials compared chlorhexidine varnish with placebo or no treatment. Data from two trials involving permanent teeth (one using 10% chlorhexidine and the other 40%) were pooled. The results showed an increase in the DMFS (Decayed, Missing, and Filled Surfaces) increment in the varnish group by 0.53 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.47 to 1.53; two trials, 690 participants; very low-quality evidence). One trial using 10% chlorhexidine varnish provided data on elevated mutans streptococci levels, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.80 to 1.07; 496 participants; very low-quality evidence). Adverse effects, such as ulcers or tooth staining, were not observed in one trial, while another trial reported no side effects. None of the trials assessed outcomes such as pain, quality of life, patient satisfaction, or costs. Two trials evaluated chlorhexidine gel (0.12% concentration) compared to no treatment in primary teeth. The results for new caries development were inconclusive, with a 95% CI compatible with either an increase or decrease in caries incidence (RR 1.00, 95% CI: 0.36 to 2.77; 487 participants; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, the data on the prevalence of mutans streptococci were inconclusive (RR 1.26, 95% CI: 0.95 to 1.66; two trials, 490 participants; very low-quality evidence). Both trials reported no adverse effects. However, neither trial assessed secondary outcomes such as pain, quality of life, patient satisfaction, or costs. In conclusion, the evidence from the eight included trials on chlorhexidine varnishes and gels is insufficient to support or refute the claim that chlorhexidine is more effective than placebo or no treatment in preventing dental caries or reducing mutans streptococci levels in children and adolescents. No trials were identified for other chlorhexidine-containing products, such as sprays, toothpastes, chewing gums, or mouthrinses. Further high-quality research is needed, particularly studies evaluating the effects of chlorhexidine on both primary and permanent teeth and exploring other chlorhexidine-based oral products.
